# Writing the piece

Before you write, ask the user for what you are missing. The user's request is never everything the user knows. Send one message with at most six questions, the most useful first. Ask only what would change the piece and what the request does not already answer. Look for these:

- **What the reader gets and what it costs them.** The terms as they touch this reader: pay, price, dates, what they keep, what they lose, what they can still do if they change their mind.
- **What answers the reader's main objection.** Name the objection this reader will raise and ask what the user has that answers it: what has already been done or offered about it, what has changed since, what the proposal leaves in place.
- **What shows the writer can deliver, or knows the reader's world.** A record, a credential, a time they did this before, someone who has checked their work or will vouch for it.
- **What the writer can commit to.** A date, a number, a named person, what happens if it is missed.
- **The reader.** Who exactly reads this, what they already think of the writer, and anything they hold against the writer, when the request does not say.
- **The names and dates the piece cannot go out without.** Who it is addressed to, who signs it, a deadline.
- **What the reader will find out anyway.** Close with one open question: is there a cost, a limit, a weak number or a past failure that the request leaves out and this reader knows or will learn?

When the answers come back, write the piece as you normally would, and hand it over. When the user does not know something, write without it and do not guess.


ARGUMENTS: Staff email from one of three partners at a 46-person architecture firm announcing the end of fully remote work: in office Tue/Wed/Thu from September 1. 15 hired fully remote in 2021-22; 4 live 2+ hours away and stay remote to end of next year, then once a week. Reasons: lost two large hospital projects at final interview, clients said team seemed not to know each other; juniors hired since 2022 taking ~30% longer to lead a project. Partners have been in one day/week, will now be in all three days. One page, emailed before Friday all-staff meeting.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will change what the email says.

1. **Dates.** Today is 16 November 2026, so I'm reading "September 1" as 1 September 2027 and "end of next year" as 31 December 2027. That gives the four long-distance staff only four months on the new rule before they start coming in weekly. Is that right?
2. **The other 11 remote hires.** They were hired on fully remote terms and now have to come in three days a week. What are you offering them, if anything? For example: help with travel costs, a later start for some of them, help with moving, or a way to talk it through one-on-one. Also, does this change their contracts? Is there anything about notice or consent that you need to say?
3. **Exceptions.** Will there be a process for people with caregiving duties, health needs or disabilities? If so, who do they contact, and by when?
4. **The office.** Is there room for all 46 people on the same three days? Are you changing anything there, such as desks, meeting rooms or the kitchen? Will Monday and Friday stay as free choice between home and office?
5. **What you'll do in person.** Do you have anything concrete planned for the in-office days? For example, mentoring pairs for juniors, design reviews, or the partners sitting with project teams. Right now the email gives reasons and asks people to come in, but it doesn't say what they'll get from coming in.
6. **Sign-off and Friday.** Should it be signed by all three partners or just you, and with which names? What time is the Friday meeting, and will there be a way to send questions in beforehand? Finally, is there anything staff will find out anyway that this leaves out? For example: someone has already been told something different, the hospital losses led to cuts, or the 30% figure is based on only a few people.

<final_document>
**Subject: Working in the studio Tuesday to Thursday from 1 September 2027**

Hi everyone,

Most of you will be affected by this change, so I'm writing before Friday's all-staff meeting to give you time to read it and think about it before we talk.

From 1 September 2027, everyone at the firm will work in the studio on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays. This means we're ending fully remote work. Fifteen of you joined us as fully remote employees in 2021 and 2022. For you, this is a real change from what you signed up for, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

**Why we're doing this**

Last year we reached the final interview for two large hospital projects and lost both. When we asked the clients why, they both said the same thing: our team seemed not to know each other. Projects like these keep a firm our size busy for years.

We see the same problem in our own review records. Junior staff hired since 2022 are taking about 30% longer to get to the point of leading a project. We believe part of the reason is that much of what prepares someone to lead is learned by sitting near people who already do it, and that's hard when we're rarely in the same room.

**What the partners will do**

Until now the partners have been in the studio one day a week, which means we haven't set the example. From 1 September, all three of us will be in Tuesday to Thursday too. Five of our six project leads already come in on those days by choice, so the people you'd most want to learn from will be there.

**What this means for you**

- **Commuting.** If you live more than 30 miles from the office, we'll pay up to $150 a month toward your commute.
- **If you live more than two hours away.** Four colleagues are in this position. You keep your current arrangement until 31 December 2027. From January 2028, you'll come in one day a week.
- **Desks.** We don't have a desk for everyone yet. New desks arrive in August, before the change begins.
- **Exceptions.** Apart from those four, we can't offer individual exceptions to the three days. I know that will be hard for some of you, and I'd rather tell you clearly now than leave it uncertain.
- **Review.** Six months in, around March 2028, we'll review how this is working, together with you.

**Questions**

We'll talk it through on Friday at 10 a.m. in the main studio. If you'd like to ask something beforehand, or in private, come to me or to HR.

Paul Whitaker
Partner
</final_document>

Before you send it, there are a few things to check:

- **Contracts and notice.** You weren't sure about these, and the email says nothing on them. The 15 remote hires will ask whether their contracts allow this. An employment lawyer or HR should confirm the answer before Friday.
- **The no-exceptions line.** I wrote it the way you described it. However, in many places employers are legally required to consider accommodation requests from people with disabilities or certain caregiving needs. Ask HR to check that sentence before it goes out. You could soften it to "beyond those four, any requests go through HR," but only if that's actually true.
- **Mondays and Fridays.** The email doesn't say anything about those days, and someone will ask on Friday. It's worth deciding before the meeting.
- **The 30% figure.** Since you don't know how many people it's based on, expect a question about it. Try to find the number before Friday.
- **Something concrete for juniors.** Right now, the only thing the email offers in return for coming in is that the partners and project leads will be there. If you can add one specific plan, such as mentoring pairs or weekly design reviews, the case for the change will be stronger.
